chunks: they stand in rows with their feet firm, reciting portions of the Qur'an, reciting it with measured recitation, creating grief for themselves through it, and seeking by it the cure for their ailments. When they pass a verse containing encouragement, they lean towards it with hope, and their souls gaze at it with longing, and they feel as if it is before their eyes. And when they pass a verse containing warning, they direct the ears of their hearts to it, and feel as if the sighing of Hell and its breathing are at the roots of their ears. So they are bent over their middles, prostrating on their foreheads, their palms, and the tips of their feet, seeking from Allah the freeing of their necks.

As for the day, they are enduring, learned, virtuous and God-fearing. Fear has made them thin like arrows. If one looks at them, he thinks they are sick, although there is no sickness in the people, and he says: They have gone mad!
ai.seo_question: What are the characteristics of the God-fearing during the night and day according to Nahj al-Balagha?
ai.summary: In Nahj al-Balagha, Imam Ali (AS) characterizes the *muttaqun* through the dichotomy of night and day, highlighting how their nocturnal *tarteel* (measured recitation) transforms abstract verses into visceral experiences of hope and fear. This spiritual intensity manifests physically during the day as a state of *hulam'* (tranquil awe), where their profound internal consciousness of God renders them outwardly still and contemplative, often mistaken for illness by the unobservant.

en.sayed-ali-raza: During a night they are upstanding on their feet reading portions of the Qur’ān and reciting it in a well-measured way, creating through it grief for themselves and seeking by it the cure for their ailments. If they come across a verse creating eagerness (for Paradise) they pursue it avidly, and their spirits turn towards it eagerly, and they feel as if it is in front of them. And when they come across a verse which contains fear (of Hell) they bend the ears of their hearts towards it, and feel as though the sound of Hell and its cries are reaching their ears. They bend themselves from their backs, prostrate themselves on their foreheads, their palms, their knees and their toes, and beseech Allāh, the Sublime, for their deliverance.

During the day they are enduring, learned, virtuous and God-fearing. Fear (of Allāh) has made them thin like arrows. If any one looks at them he believes they are sick, although they are not sick, and he says that they have gone mad.
